Intestinal gases cannot be eliminated due to the high density of meconium and its adhesion to the intestinal walls, so that the abdomen becomes intensely weathered, occlusive, but in the absence of air–fluid levels. The abdominal radiograph has almost the same appearance in the supine and erect position with distended loops without air–fluid levels and a ground glass or ‘soap-bubble’ appearance (Neuhauser’s sign) (Figure 3). Another typical occurrence on X-ray is inspissated pellets along the large intestine wall. If there is a total obstruction, there might not be any air in the rectum.

in_text_mentions: imple MI, with bilious vomiting, marked abdominal distension, abdominal wall edema, fever (Figure 6). Respiratory distress may also be caused by substantial abdominal distention. If the neonate is stable, a diagnostic contrast enema can help identify malrotation by pinpointing the cecum’s location and identify a microcolon caused by proximal obstruction in the terminal ileum. If the patient’s clinical condition is deteriorated, a simple abdominal X-ray (Figure 7) and an ultrasound are sufficient to guide operative management. Anyway, infants with complicated MI will always require surgery [8].

The colour of the involved segment was dark and appeared congested (Fig. 2). The volvulus was corrected by untwisting the mesentery. The involved gut was hugely distended due to the presence of thick tenacious meconium. The thick meconium was concentrated in distal small bowel whereas the colon was packed with small beads. plate_findings.evidence: contrast agent stopping at the inflated, distended small intestine

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (a, b). a: The figure shows an abdominal X-ray (radiograph) where contrast agent has stopped in the dilated small intestine, which is a classic diagnostic presentation of meconium ileus, supported by the figure caption and in-text mentions. b: The figure shows an abdominal X-ray (radiograph) for Twin II. The caption states the diagnostics were similar to Twin I, who showed contrast stopping in a distended small intestine, indicating meconium ileus.
panels.attribution_text: Puzik et al. Lethal course of meconium ileus in preterm twins revealing a novel cystic fibrosis mutation (p.Cys524Tyr).. BMC pediatrics 2014. doi:10.1186/1471-2431-14-13. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 1.
panels.figure_caption: Initial X-rays of both twins. Chest and abdominal X-ray with contrast agent upon initial presentation of twin I (a) and II (b) showing contrast agent stopping at the inflated, distended small intestine next to signs of neonatal respiratory distress syndrome.
in_text_mentions: Twin I displayed good cardiopulmonary adaptation (Apgar score 7/9/9). Upon signs of ileus contrast X-ray of the abdomen (administration per gastric tube) showed immotility of the gut with contrast agent stopping at the inflated, distended small intestine on day 5 (see Figure 1a).

Twin II developed respiratory failure after birth necessitating mechanical ventilation and surfactant administration (Apgar score 3/7/7). Diagnostics on admission to our unit were similar compared to twin I (see Figure 1b).
